content: 1. During the spraying process, if the operator remains inside the cabin, neither inhalation nor dermal exposure is anticipated. However, exposure is assumed to occur during the mixing and loading of insecticides, as well as during the washing and maintenance of the equipment. 2. Using empty product containers to store food or drinking water can result in significant exposure and even acute intoxications. The variability of such practices is high, and the associated risks cannot be effectively modeled. These misuses are not included in this risk assessment. 3. Space spraying is typically organized by authorities, and it is assumed that residents rarely have access to empty containers. 4. The frequency of indoor space spraying treatments varies widely depending on the exposure scenario and geographical location, ranging from annual or occasional treatments to repeated applications during epidemic situations or disease outbreaks. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends spraying every 2–3 days for a week in emergency situations, followed by 1–2 sprays per week. A default of 15 spraying incidents per year is used, but local, case-specific data should be utilized whenever possible. 5. It is assumed that WHO guidelines are followed, meaning residents are not present in the house during spraying, they remain outside until the spray has settled or degraded, and all food items are removed before spraying begins. 6. Residents, including adults and children, are assumed to be exposed dermally by touching contaminated surfaces in treated houses or by ingesting contaminated food or water. Surface contamination and subsequent dermal exposure to settled residues are assumed to occur as the spray deposits on horizontal surfaces such as tables, work surfaces, and floors. 7. In a worst-case scenario, all sprayed material is deposited on horizontal surfaces. However, in practice, only about 50% of droplets settle on surfaces due to factors like wind, with smaller droplets escaping through openings. Residues on surfaces are expected to decay or be removed quickly, resulting in acute exposure. 8. For outdoor space spraying, bystanders are assumed to be exposed for 15 minutes. Algorithms are used to estimate exposure and absorbed doses caused by indoor or outdoor space spraying of insecticides. 9. During mixing and loading of insecticide formulations, inhalation exposure is not considered significant, but dermal exposure must be accounted for. The formulations used in space spraying are all liquids, such as hot-fogging concentrates, ultra-low-volume liquids, emulsions, oil-in-water formulations, and emulsifiable concentrates. 10. In the absence of formulation-specific data, default values for dermal exposure to liquid formulations during mixing and loading are used. Systemic dose estimation from mixing and loading is presented in specific calculation models. 11. Inhalation exposure during application is assumed to be significant in scenarios where no respiratory protective equipment (RPE) is used. In guideline scenarios, efficient RPE and good work practices can provide up to 90% protection. 12. During indoor spraying, the operator remains in the contaminated area, while in outdoor spraying with hand-held equipment, the operator is assumed to stay outside the fog as much as possible but may still be within the fog for 30 minutes per day. In vehicle-mounted spraying, a closed cabin with air filtering is assumed, and no inhalation exposure is expected. 13. Dermal exposure during application and equipment maintenance is significant in lax scenarios where protective clothing is not used. In guideline scenarios, protective clothing and gloves reduce dermal exposure to 10% of that in lax scenarios. 14. Residential exposure is assumed to result from dermal contact with spray residues on furniture, shelves, and floors, as well as ingestion of contaminated food or water. For toxic products excreted in breast milk, this may be an important exposure route for newborns. 15. Residents are instructed not to enter houses during or immediately after spraying, so inhalation exposure is assumed to be limited to outdoor applications. Bystanders or residents may spend 15 minutes in the spray. 16. Ingestion exposure results from consuming contaminated foodstuffs. It is assumed that food is not directly sprayed but becomes contaminated through transfer from sprayed surfaces. Default assumptions include an 8% transfer rate from contaminated surfaces to food items. 17. Toddler hand-to-mouth activity is a significant route of exposure, as toddlers frequently put objects in their mouths and ingest soil or dust from contaminated hands. Default values for pesticide transfer and extraction by saliva are used to estimate ingestion exposure. 18. Exposure via breast milk is estimated for newborns as a worst-case scenario. If the estimated dose for the newborn is significant, exposure is also estimated for infants. When data on excretion in milk are unavailable, an upper bound of exposure can be estimated based on the physicochemical characteristics and kinetics of the insecticide. 19. Total systemic dose is calculated by summing contributions from different exposure routes. Risk assessments should be conducted for operators, residents (adults and children), and bystanders in the sprayed area. 20. Risk characterization involves evaluating the probability of adverse effects under defined exposure conditions. This includes comparing time-weighted average exposure estimates with tolerable systemic doses. If risk ratios exceed 1, health risks may be unacceptable, and operational conditions or product formulations may need to be adjusted. 21. Environmental risk assessment is complex and multifaceted, with regional and national guidelines available but no globally established system. This document does not propose a single scheme for international harmonization.
